KEY MESSAGE 1...Seasonably cool today ahead of a powerful
coastal low set to bring hazardous weather on Thanksgiving Day.

A strong dome of Canadian high pressure currently stretches from
the Great Lakes into southern Quebec and New England. The
influence of this ridge axis extends all the way down into the
Florida Panhandle. Clouds will continue to expand northward 
into the Mid-Atlantic region today, keeping temperatures a touch
below normal. This all sets to the stages for a period of 
hazardous weather tonight into Thanksgiving Day.

There are two key components aloft to consider for this major
pattern change ahead. Multi-channel water vapor imagery depicts
an upper low spinning across the Midwest. A separate feature 
off to the south is currently pushing across the lower
Mississippi Valley while taking an eastward track toward the 
Gulf Coast. This more southern disturbance is the one that 
begins to gain latitude along the southeastern U.S. coast while 
attaining a negative tilt. This strengthening process will yield
a series of deepening cyclone centers along a wavy occluding 
frontal system. Based on late November climatology, this trough 
exhibits highly anomalous parameters which include its moisture 
content, wind fields, and degree of low-level convergence. This 
high- impact system is expected to impact the local area late 
tonight through Thanksgiving Day.

The intense wind field extends all the way down to the surface
layer. Most guidance even shows 70 to 80 knot wind vectors down
to the 925-mb level. The main question is can any of the gusty
showers bring this intense wind field down to the surface.
Forecast soundings show ample stability in the lower atmosphere,
but a few rogue gusts approaching 65 to 75 mph are not out of 
the question. With the strong winds in place, an array of High 
Wind Warnings and Wind Advisories have been issued. These 
generally cover the morning to afternoon hours on Thanksgiving 
Day. Most of the region can expect sustained winds of 25 to 30 
mph with gusts to around 50 to 55 mph. All wind products expire 
by the late afternoon to near sunset. 

Besides the wind, a moderate to heavy area of rain lifts 
northward across the area. This first impacts the I-64 corridor 
in the 3-9 AM window, with I-66 around 5-11 AM, and finally 
I-70 by 6 AM-noon. Rain totals of 1 to 2 inches may fall as 
this activity pushes through. Some sensitive locations could see
spotty flooding issues if the higher amount is realized. Once 
this shifts activity lifts north of the Mason-Dixon Line,
precipitation turns more scattered in nature as the upper 
trough passes overhead. Amidst all the wind and rain, 
temperatures should be on the cooler side due to prevailing 
northeasterly winds. Expect highs in the 50s with mainly 40s 
west of the Blue Ridge. Heading into the night, thick low clouds
will hold temperatures in the upper 30s to 40s.

The northern upper low eventually crosses the region by early 
Friday. Ample lift underneath this feature will bring some 
scattered showers on Friday morning. On the back side of the 
trough, some upslope rain/snow showers are expected along the 
Allegheny Front. It is not the most favorable wind direction 
which is just south of the west. Perhaps an inch of snow is 
possible across the higher peaks. For the entire area, winds 
remain elevated with gusts up to 25 to 35 mph, locally nearing 
45 mph in the mountains. The westerly component to the winds 
does help warm temperatures back into the 50s. Cyclonic 
gradients remain tight into Friday night as lows fall into the 
30s to low 40s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions anticipated this weekend before
additional precipitation chances return early next week.

A brief period of ridging in the immediate aftermath of the coastal 
low will bring clearing clouds and diminishing winds Saturday & 
into Sunday. Temperatures will remain seasonable during this period, 
with daytime highs in the 40s and 50s and overnight lows generally 
in the 30s. Winds temporarily shift west to southwest through the 
weekend, with gusts up to 25-35 mph Saturday afternoon and 15-25 
mph Sunday afternoon. 

Winds shift back northwesterly Monday, accompanied by increasing 
cloud cover as the upper-level pattern shifts back to troughing over 
the Ohio River Valley before shifting east. Temperatures likely 
remain seasonable during this period, but precipitation chances will 
increase again as this troughing moves through the Mid-Atlantic. 
There is some uncertainty still regarding when exactly this system 
will bring impacts to the region, but overall the general consensus 
seems to be to anticipate further precipitation in the Nov 30-Dec 
2 timeframe as potentially a couple disturbances move through. As 
drought has been creeping back into the region from the extended dry 
weather earlier this month, any flooding concerns will likely remain
